title: Hagar and the God Who Sees
summary: Weary of waiting, Sarai gives Hagar to Abram; strife drives Hagar into the wilderness, where the LORD finds, hears, and sends her back.
historicalContext: Ten years after entering Canaan, Abram and Sarai still had no child, though the covenant of chapter 15 had promised an heir from Abram’s own body. Hagar, an Egyptian slave woman, probably entered the household during the sojourn in Egypt (12:16). Law collections from Mesopotamia show that a childless wife could give her female slave to her husband and count the resulting children as her own, and they also regulated the friction such an arrangement predictably caused. Abram and Sarai were therefore acting within the accepted customs of their homeland. The way to Shur ran from the Negev toward the fortified frontier of Egypt, and Hagar, fleeing her mistress, was heading home along it. Kadesh lay on the southern edge of Canaan’s wilderness, near the region where Abram often moved his flocks (20:1). Bered is otherwise unknown, and the well cannot now be located with certainty.
literaryContext: Genesis 16 stands between two covenant scenes: the promise sealed among the divided animals (chapter 15) and the covenant of circumcision with its renaming of Abram and Sarai (chapter 17). Placed there, it shows what happens when the heirs of promise try to supply by their own arrangement what God has pledged to give. The chapter falls into two halves. In verses 1–6 the human characters speak and act while God is mentioned but silent; in verses 7–14 the Angel of the LORD takes the initiative, questions, commands, promises, and names. A frame of births encloses the whole: Sarai “bare him no children” (v. 1), and Hagar “bare Abram a son” (v. 15). Echoes of Eden (“hearkened to the voice,” “took … and gave”) and anticipations of the exodus (affliction, flight, a God who hears) give this household quarrel a significance far beyond its tents.
themes: Impatience that tries to secure God’s promise by human means
Domestic strife as the fruit of a faithless plan
The LORD who seeks out the outcast and hears affliction
The Angel of the LORD who speaks as God
Mercy extended beyond the line of the covenant heir
Waiting faith and God’s appointed time

outline.title: Sarai’s Plan for an Heir
outline.summary: After ten years without a child, Sarai gives her Egyptian maid to Abram, and he agrees.

outline.title: Contempt, Blame, and Harshness
outline.summary: Hagar’s pregnancy turns the household upside down; Sarai blames Abram, he yields, and her harsh treatment drives Hagar away.

outline.title: The Angel of the LORD Finds Hagar
outline.summary: At a spring on the road to Egypt the LORD’s Angel questions Hagar, sends her back, promises many descendants, and names her unborn son.

outline.title: The God Who Sees
outline.summary: Hagar names the LORD who spoke to her, and the well becomes a lasting memorial of his seeing care.

outline.title: Ishmael Born to Abram
outline.summary: Hagar bears a son whom Abram names Ishmael, at eighty-six years of age.

verses.bibleText: Now Sarai Abram's wife bare him no children: and she had an handmaid, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter opens on the problem that has hung over Abram’s story since Genesis 11:30. “Now Sarai Abram’s wife bare him no children.” The previous chapter ended with a solemn covenant and the assurance that Abram’s heir would come “out of thine own bowels” (15:4), yet the tent is still silent. Beside Sarai, “Abram’s wife,” the narrator now sets another woman.

“She had an handmaid, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar.” The introduction is brief but loaded. Hagar belongs to Sarai, not to Abram; she is a foreigner; and she comes from Egypt, the land where Abram’s fear once put Sarai into Pharaoh’s house (12:10–20). Among the servants Pharaoh gave Abram on that occasion (12:16) there was very likely this young woman. A decision born of fear in Egypt had left behind a quiet consequence that now becomes the occasion of a new failure.

The contrast is deliberate. One woman has status and no child; the other has no status but, as the story will show, conceives at once. Genesis repeatedly lets the promise hang on a barren womb (Rebekah, Rachel) so that the heir will be seen as God’s gift. Sarai’s barrenness is not an accident in the plot but the stage on which God means to display his power. The tragedy of the chapter lies in a couple who misread the delay as a dead end.

wordNotes.explanation: A female slave or maidservant, usually attached personally to her mistress rather than to the household at large. Leah and Rachel each receive such a servant from their father (Genesis 29:24, 29), and the same word appears when they later give them to Jacob. The term marks Hagar’s dependence; she has no power to refuse what her mistress decides. In Galatians Paul calls her the “bondwoman,” translating the idea with the Greek paidiskē.

verses.bibleText: And Sarai said unto Abram, Behold now, the LORD hath restrained me from bearing: I pray thee, go in unto my maid; it may be that I may obtain children by her. And Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Sarai speaks first, and her words reveal both piety and weariness. “Behold now, the LORD hath restrained me from bearing.” She rightly sees the LORD as sovereign over the womb; Scripture elsewhere speaks the same way of God closing and opening it (20:18; 30:2; 1 Samuel 1:5). Yet her confession leads to the wrong conclusion. If the LORD has restrained her, she reasons, then the promise must come some other way, and she will supply it. Faith would have said, “If the LORD has closed, the LORD can open,” and waited.

Her proposal followed recognized custom. Ancient Near Eastern marriage contracts and law collections allowed a childless wife to give her slave to her husband so that the offspring could be counted as the wife’s. Sarai is not inventing something shameful in the eyes of her contemporaries; she is reaching for the respectable solution of her culture. That is precisely what makes the scene instructive. The danger to faith is not always an outrageous sin. Often it is the reasonable, socially approved method that quietly replaces trust in what God has said. Her own words carry the uncertainty: “it may be that I may obtain children by her.” Where God had spoken a sure word, Sarai can only offer a hopeful “perhaps.”

Neither Sarai nor Abram ever addresses Hagar or uses her name. She is spoken of as “my maid,” an instrument for someone else’s purpose. The narrative does not hide that this is how she is treated, and the second half of the chapter will answer it when the LORD calls her by name.

“And Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai.” The phrase deliberately recalls Genesis 3:17, where Adam “hearkened unto the voice of thy wife” and took the forbidden fruit. Listening to one’s wife is not wrong in itself; in 21:12 God tells Abraham to heed Sarah. The fault lies in heeding a voice that leads away from the word of God. Abram had believed the LORD and it was counted to him for righteousness (15:6), yet genuine faith can still falter under long delay. God did not need Abram’s device. He needed his trust.

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “I shall be built up.” The verb banah (to build) is used of establishing a household, and Hebrew hearers would catch the sound-play with ben, “son.” Sarai hopes that a child born through Hagar will build her house. Rachel uses identical language when she gives Bilhah to Jacob. The expression is idiomatic and should not be pressed into a theology of “building,” but it shows that Sarai counts the child as hers and sees the family line as the thing at stake.

From ʿatsar, “to shut up, hold back.” The same verb describes the LORD closing the wombs of Abimelech’s household. Sarai’s use of it is theologically correct: life comes from God. Her error is not her theology of providence but her decision to act around it.

verses.bibleText: And Sarai Abram's wife took Hagar her maid the Egyptian, after Abram had dwelt ten years in the land of Canaan, and gave her to her husband Abram to be his wife.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrator slows the action and repeats every title: Sarai is “Abram’s wife,” Hagar is “her maid the Egyptian,” and Abram is “her husband.” Each relationship is spelled out, as though to underline how tangled the household is about to become. The verbs “took” and “gave” echo Genesis 3:6, where the woman took the fruit and gave it to her husband. The parallel is restrained but real: once again a wife takes the initiative, a husband consents, and a choice that seemed to promise good opens the door to grief.

The time note matters. It was “after Abram had dwelt ten years in the land of Canaan.” Abram was seventy-five when he left Haran (12:4); he is now about eighty-five, and Sarai seventy-five. A decade of waiting in the land of promise, with no visible progress, is the setting of this decision. Scripture is honest that delay tests faith severely. The same delay, however, was part of God’s purpose. The heir would come when human possibility was entirely exhausted, so that no one could mistake the gift for nature’s achievement (Romans 4:19–21).

Hagar is given to Abram “to be his wife.” The Hebrew word is the ordinary term for wife, though later texts call her a concubine (25:6). Her standing was secondary but real, and her child would be Abram’s son. Genesis 2:24 had described marriage as one man and one woman becoming one flesh; every instance of plural marriage in Genesis brings rivalry and sorrow, and this one is no exception. The narrative passes no explicit verdict here. It lets the consequences speak.

wordNotes.explanation: ʾIshshah is the common word for “woman” or “wife.” Genesis uses it for Hagar here and for Bilhah and Keturah elsewhere, while other passages call the same women pilegesh, “concubine.” In the patriarchal setting the two terms overlap, describing a subordinate wife whose children belonged to the family. The term confers real obligations on Abram toward Hagar, which makes his later passivity the more striking.

verses.bibleText: And he went in unto Hagar, and she conceived: and when she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The plan works at once, and its success is the beginning of its failure. “He went in unto Hagar, and she conceived.” The verb sequence is brisk, without word of affection or reluctance. What Sarai could not achieve in decades happens immediately for her servant, and the reversal exposes the pain that the arrangement was meant to ease.

“When she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes.” In a culture where fruitfulness was counted a mark of blessing and barrenness a reproach (30:1, 23; 1 Samuel 1:6), Hagar’s pregnancy instantly altered the balance of honour in the tent. Sarai had expected Hagar to remain a servant who would bear a child on her behalf. Hagar, carrying the patriarch’s heir, now regards her mistress as of little account. Ancient law collections anticipated exactly this situation, permitting a mistress to put a slave back in her place if she claimed equality after bearing children. The friction was so familiar that Proverbs lists “an handmaid that is heir to her mistress” among the things under which the earth cannot bear up (Proverbs 30:21, 23).

The verb translated “despised” is the same root used in 12:3 for those who curse or treat Abram lightly. The narrator may be hinting that in belittling the mother of the promise Hagar sets herself against the line of blessing, as Lot drifted from it before her. Yet the fault is not hers alone. She had been taken, given, and used without consultation. Pride in her, hurt in Sarai, and passivity in Abram combine to show that once God’s pattern for marriage and his timing for the promise are set aside, every person in the household is diminished.

wordNotes.explanation: From qalal, “to be light, slight,” hence “to be of little account.” In her eyes Sarai had become lightweight, of diminished worth. The intensive form of the same root means “to curse” in Genesis 12:3, where God warns that he will curse whoever treats Abram with contempt. The word does not necessarily imply open insult; it describes a change of regard, a lowering of Sarai in Hagar’s estimation.

verses.bibleText: And Sarai said unto Abram, My wrong be upon thee: I have given my maid into thy bosom; and when she saw that she had conceived, I was despised in her eyes: the LORD judge between me and thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Sarai turns not on Hagar but on Abram. “My wrong be upon thee.” The word she uses for “wrong” is ḥamas, the violence and lawlessness that filled the earth before the flood (6:11). She feels herself the victim of an outrage, and she holds her husband responsible. The irony is plain: the arrangement was her idea, and she says so in the next breath, “I have given my maid into thy bosom.” Like the first woman and the first man in Genesis 3:12–13, she shifts the blame.

Her complaint is not entirely unjust, however. Abram was the head of the household and the only one who could protect the rights of his first wife or restrain the pride of his second. Sarai’s accusation implies that he had allowed the new situation to stand, perhaps even that he had welcomed the attention of the woman who would give him a son. The repetition of the narrator’s own words, “I was despised in her eyes,” suggests that Sarai has read Hagar’s attitude correctly.

“The LORD judge between me and thee.” Sarai appeals to a higher court, the kind of oath used when one party believes the other has failed in duty (31:53; 1 Samuel 24:12). Whether the appeal is a cry of faith or an angry flourish is debated; spoken in the heat of the moment to her own husband, it carries more irritation than prayer. It is striking that throughout the chapter Sarai speaks about the LORD twice but never speaks to him, and the narrative never records the LORD speaking to her here. The household that had the promises has, for the moment, lost the habit of bringing its troubles to God.

wordNotes.explanation: Ḥamas denotes violent wrong, injustice that violates what is right. It names the corruption that brought the flood and the injury the psalmist suffers from false witnesses. Sarai’s choice of so strong a word shows how deeply she feels the humiliation. Grammatically the phrase may be read either as a curse (“may my wrong be on you”) or as a charge (“the wrong done to me is your responsibility”); either way, she lays the burden on Abram.

verses.bibleText: But Abram said unto Sarai, Behold, thy maid is in thy hand; do to her as it pleaseth thee. And when Sarai dealt hardly with her, she fled from her face.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abram’s reply sounds conciliatory but abdicates responsibility. “Behold, thy maid is in thy hand; do to her as it pleaseth thee.” He restores Hagar to Sarai’s authority, acknowledging that the original household order should not have been overturned. Ancient custom allowed a mistress to reduce an insolent slave-wife to the rank of servant, though not to sell her, and Abram appears to follow that provision. Yet Hagar is now his wife and is carrying his child. By washing his hands of her he leaves the vulnerable party without protection. He avoids her name, as Sarai did, calling her only “thy maid.” The man who would later intercede boldly for Sodom (18:23–32) does not speak a word on behalf of the woman in his own tent.

“And when Sarai dealt hardly with her, she fled from her face.” The verb is ʿanah, “to afflict, oppress, humble.” It is the word God used in 15:13 for what Egypt would do to Abram’s descendants, and Exodus uses it for the Egyptian taskmasters (Exodus 1:11–12). Here the roles are startlingly reversed: the mother of Israel afflicts an Egyptian, and the Egyptian flees. The narrator does not soften Sarai’s conduct. Whatever Hagar’s pride, the response was harsh enough to drive a pregnant woman into the desert.

At this point every human relationship in the household has broken. Sarai has despised Abram’s judgment, Hagar has despised Sarai, Sarai has afflicted Hagar, and Abram has refused to act. The plan that was meant to build Sarai’s house has emptied it. Scripture tells the failures of the patriarchs openly because the promise does not rest on their virtue. It rests on the faithfulness of God, who is about to step into the story where every human actor has failed.

The scene also gives a sober warning to all who hold power over others. Those who have been wounded easily become wounders, and authority exercised in resentment does lasting harm. The law of Moses would later command Israel not to afflict the stranger, remembering that they had been strangers in Egypt (Exodus 22:21–23).

wordNotes.explanation: The intensive stem of ʿanah, “to afflict, humiliate, treat harshly.” It can describe physical or social mistreatment and is used of Egypt’s oppression of Israel. The word will return twice in the chapter: the Angel tells Hagar to “submit” (the reflexive form of the same verb, v. 9), and the LORD names her son because he has heard her “affliction” (a related noun, v. 11). The thread binds the chapter together: the harshness Hagar suffered is fully known to God.

Baraḥ means to run away, to flee in haste. Jacob will flee from Esau and from Laban, Moses from Pharaoh, and Israel from Egypt. Hagar’s flight places her among those whom God meets precisely when they run.

verses.bibleText: And the angel of the LORD found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain in the way to Shur.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The turn in the chapter comes with a new subject. Until now the human characters have planned, spoken, and acted, while God has only been mentioned. Now “the angel of the LORD found her.” This is the first appearance in Scripture of the figure called the Angel of the LORD, and he appears not to the patriarch but to a runaway Egyptian slave. The God whom Sarai had blamed for her barrenness is the One who goes after the woman she drove away.

The verb “found” is significant. When God is the subject and a person the object, finding implies purposeful seeking rather than chance discovery. Moses would later say that the LORD “found” Israel “in a desert land” and kept him as the apple of his eye (Deuteronomy 32:10). Hagar did not go looking for God; he came looking for her. That initiative is the heart of the gospel long before the gospel is preached in full: “the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10).

Who is this Angel? The Hebrew word malʾak means “messenger,” and many angels serve God in that role. Yet this messenger speaks with the authority of God himself. He will promise in the first person, “I will multiply thy seed” (v. 10), a pledge only God can make, and Hagar will name him as the LORD who spoke to her (v. 13). The same pattern recurs when the Angel of the LORD speaks from the burning bush and then declares, “I am the God of thy father” (Exodus 3:2–6), and when Jacob blesses Joseph’s sons in the name of “the Angel which redeemed me from all evil” (48:16; Hosea 12:4–5). At the same time he is distinguished from the LORD who sends him (v. 11). This combination of identity and distinction is best understood as an appearance of the pre-incarnate Son, the One who has always made the invisible Father known (John 1:18). The text itself does not elaborate, and it should not be overloaded, but it plainly presents a divine messenger through whom the LORD himself was present.

The setting is precise: “by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain in the way to Shur.” Shur, meaning “wall,” probably refers to the line of fortifications on Egypt’s eastern frontier (25:18; Exodus 15:22). Hagar was going home. Alone, pregnant, and far from the tents, she had reached a spring on the caravan route, and there, at the edge of her old world, she was met.

wordNotes.term: מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה (malʾak YHWH) — the angel of the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: Malʾak denotes a messenger, human or heavenly. Joined to the divine name in a definite construction, it designates a particular messenger who represents the LORD so fully that he speaks as God and is addressed as God, while also being sent by God. In Genesis he appears here and in 22:11–18, and he is closely linked with “the Angel” Jacob confesses as his Redeemer. The Septuagint renders the phrase angelos kyriou. Malachi’s promise of “the messenger of the covenant” uses the same noun.

From matsaʾ, “to find.” With God as subject and a person as object, the verb often carries the sense of a deliberate, gracious encounter, as when God “found” David his servant. It points to divine initiative toward one who could not reach him.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go? And she said, I flee from the face of my mistress Sarai.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Hagar, Sarai’s maid.” For the first time in the chapter someone addresses Hagar, and he calls her by name. Sarai and Abram spoke only of “my maid” and “thy maid”; the Angel of the LORD speaks to her as a person. At the same time he identifies her accurately as “Sarai’s maid,” reminding her of the household relationship from which she has fled. Grace and truth arrive together.

The twofold question, “whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go?”, is not a request for information the Angel lacks; he already knows her name, her status, and her mistress. Like God’s questions to Adam (“Where art thou?” 3:9) and to Cain (“Where is Abel thy brother?” 4:9), and like his later question to Elijah under the juniper tree (“What doest thou here?” 1 Kings 19:9), it invites the person to face where she is and what she is doing.

Hagar answers honestly but only in part: “I flee from the face of my mistress Sarai.” She knows what she is running from. She says nothing about where she is going, perhaps because she has no plan beyond escape, perhaps because the road to Shur led back to Egypt and its gods. Her silence on the second question is eloquent.

Notice that she calls Sarai “my mistress.” Even in flight she has not escaped the relationship. The Angel will not pretend otherwise, but he will give her a future that Sarai could not take away.

wordNotes.explanation: Gevereth is the feminine counterpart of gevir, “lord, master,” and denotes a woman with authority over servants. Proverbs uses it in the saying about a handmaid who displaces her mistress, and Isaiah uses it of Babylon as “the lady of kingdoms.” Hagar’s use of the title shows that she still recognizes Sarai’s rightful authority over her even while fleeing it.

verses.bibleText: And the angel of the LORD said unto her, Return to thy mistress, and submit thyself under her hands.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The first command is hard. “Return to thy mistress, and submit thyself under her hands.” The Angel does not take Hagar to Egypt or provide her a new home in the desert. He sends her back to the very place where she suffered.

Two words carry the weight. “Return” (shuv) is the common Old Testament word for turning back, and it often carries the sense of repentance, of turning from a wrong course to the right one. “Submit thyself” uses the reflexive form of ʿanah, the same verb that described Sarai’s harsh treatment in verse 6. Hagar is to humble herself under the hand that humbled her. Read alone, the command can seem cruel. Read in context, it addresses Hagar’s own part in the conflict: she had despised her mistress (v. 4), and the path forward begins with laying down that contempt. It also reflects the practical reality that the child she carried was Abram’s son and that his future, humanly speaking, lay within Abram’s household rather than as a fatherless fugitive in Egypt.

The command does not approve Sarai’s harshness. The same God who sends Hagar back has just announced that he has seen her affliction, and in verse 11 he will name her son for it. God holds those in authority accountable for how they use it, but he rarely commissions the one who is suffering to settle the account by flight or retaliation. Scripture repeatedly calls servants to show meekness, entrusting their cause to God (1 Peter 2:18–23), and that counsel stands alongside clear commands to masters to deal justly (Colossians 4:1). Paul did something similar when he sent the runaway Onesimus back to Philemon, but with a letter that transformed the relationship (Philemon 1:12, 16).

This verse should never be used to keep a person in danger or to excuse abuse. Hagar was not sent back alone with nothing; she returned carrying a divine promise, a revealed name for her son, and the knowledge that the LORD saw her. Obedience became possible because grace came first. The Christian reader sees the same pattern in Christ, who “when he was reviled, reviled not again” but “committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” (1 Peter 2:23).

wordNotes.explanation: The feminine imperative of shuv, “to turn back, return.” The verb can describe simple physical return, but it is also the main Old Testament word for repentance, turning from one direction to another. Both senses are present: Hagar is to go back to the household and to turn from the contempt that helped create the breach. Solomon’s prayer joins this verb with ʿanah (“afflict, humble”) when describing Israel’s repentance.

The reflexive stem of ʿanah: “humble yourself, accept affliction.” It is the same root as “dealt hardly” in verse 6. The phrase “under her hands” denotes placing oneself within another’s authority. The Angel’s words deliberately take up the vocabulary of Hagar’s suffering and turn it into a call to humility before God.

verses.bibleText: And the angel of the LORD said unto her, I will multiply thy seed exceedingly, that it shall not be numbered for multitude.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Command is followed at once by promise. “I will multiply thy seed exceedingly, that it shall not be numbered for multitude.” The speaker, the Angel of the LORD, uses the first person for what only God can do. The promise echoes, almost word for word, what God had said to Abram (13:16; 15:5) and would later repeat to Abraham on Moriah through the same Angel (22:17). Hagar is the only woman in Genesis to receive such a promise of innumerable descendants directly from God.

The pledge is remarkable for its recipient. A pregnant foreign slave in flight receives a promise ordinarily reserved for patriarchs. God had promised Abram that his seed would be multiplied without restricting the promise to Sarai’s children, and he keeps his word to the letter in Ishmael’s line. The fulfilment is traced in Genesis 25:12–18, where Ishmael’s twelve princely sons are listed, and confirmed in 17:20 and 21:13, 18.

Yet the promise of numbers is not the promise of the covenant line. Genesis 17 will make clear that the covenant is established with Isaac (17:19–21), and Paul draws on that distinction in Romans 9:7–8: “in Isaac shall thy seed be called.” Ishmael receives real blessing, providential care, and a great nation, but the line of the promised Seed who would bless all nations runs through the child of promise. God’s choice of one line for redemptive purpose does not make him indifferent to others. The God who keeps covenant with Abraham is generous beyond the covenant’s boundaries.

wordNotes.term: הַרְבָּה אַרְבֶּה (harbah arbeh) — I will multiply exceedingly
wordNotes.explanation: An infinitive absolute followed by a finite form of the same verb, raba, “to be many, increase.” The construction intensifies the promise: “I will surely, greatly multiply.” The identical construction appears in God’s oath to Abraham after the binding of Isaac. Its use for Hagar places her son within the scope of the blessing God attached to Abram’s offspring.

verses.bibleText: And the angel of the LORD said unto her, Behold, thou art with child, and shalt bear a son, and shalt call his name Ishmael; because the LORD hath heard thy affliction.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The third speech of the Angel takes the form of a birth announcement, the first in Scripture. “Behold, thou art with child, and shalt bear a son, and shalt call his name Ishmael.” The pattern of address, announcement of a son, naming, and explanation of the name will recur for Isaac (17:19), Samson (Judges 13:3–5), and, in the New Testament, for John the Baptist (Luke 1:13) and Jesus (Matthew 1:21; Luke 1:31). That Hagar’s son should be named by God before birth honours both mother and child. The boy whom Sarai meant to claim as her own receives his identity from heaven.

The name Ishmael means “God hears.” The explanation is given at once: “because the LORD hath heard thy affliction.” The word “affliction” (ʿoni) belongs to the same family as “dealt hardly” (v. 6) and “submit thyself” (v. 9). The harshness Hagar suffered was not hidden from God. Every time the boy’s name was spoken in Abram’s camp, it would testify that the God of the household had listened to the cry of its least powerful member.

This is the language of the exodus. Centuries later God would tell Moses, “I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry” (Exodus 3:7), and Israel would remember that “the LORD heard our voice, and looked on our affliction” (Deuteronomy 26:7). Here, before Israel exists, the same God hears an Egyptian afflicted by Israel’s matriarch. His compassion is not confined by nation or status.

The name El in Ishmael and the divine name LORD in the explanation stand side by side without tension. The God who hears is the covenant God of Abram. Hagar had not prayed aloud in the narrative; the text says simply that the LORD heard her affliction. God hears the misery itself, even when the sufferer has no words.

wordNotes.explanation: A sentence name joining the verb shamaʿ, “to hear,” with El, “God”: “God hears” or “may God hear.” The angelic explanation ties it to a past act, “the LORD hath heard.” Samuel’s name receives a similar explanation using the divine name LORD. Ishmael’s name is a standing confession of God’s attentive mercy.

A noun from ʿanah, meaning misery, humiliation, oppression. Leah uses it when naming Reuben, and Israel’s confession of the exodus employs it for bondage in Egypt. In this chapter it gathers up Hagar’s mistreatment and assures her that God has taken full notice of it.

verses.bibleText: And he will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man's hand against him; and he shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The announcement continues in poetic lines describing the son’s character and destiny. “He will be a wild man” translates a vivid Hebrew phrase, literally “a wild ass of a man.” The wild ass, or onager, was the untameable donkey of the steppe, fleet, hardy, and contemptuous of the town. Job pictures it scorning “the multitude of the city” and ranging the mountains for pasture (Job 39:5–8). The image is not first of all an insult. To a slave woman who had known only the will of others, it promised a son who would bow to no master. Ishmael would live free in the open country, beyond the reach of any Sarai.

The freedom would have a cost. “His hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him.” The idiom describes a life of mutual conflict, of raids given and received, typical of independent desert tribes. The final line, “he shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren,” is literally “upon the face of all his brothers.” The expression can mean simply “alongside” or “to the east of,” but in several places it carries the sense of “in defiance of” or “over against” (Deuteronomy 21:16). Genesis 25:18 uses the same words at Ishmael’s death, noting that his descendants settled from Havilah to Shur and lived in opposition to their kin. The oracle thus traces the path of Ishmael and the tribes who descended from him: numerous, independent, never subdued, and often at odds with Israel.

The history of the Ishmaelite peoples confirmed the word God spoke here, and their long independence in the deserts of Arabia stands as a witness to his providential care for them. Yet the verse must be read with care. It describes Ishmael and his line in the biblical setting; it is not a key for judging modern nations or a warrant for disparaging Arab or Muslim neighbours, many of whom share neither descent nor way of life with the tribes of Genesis. The same God who foretold Ishmael’s turbulent life also promised to bless him (17:20).

The conflict foretold also mirrors the household from which it sprang. A child conceived in rivalry would grow into a man of rivalry. Choices made in impatience echo for generations, and the tension between Ishmael and Isaac would surface again in 21:9. Even so, the Scriptures look toward a day when the sons of Ishmael’s line, Kedar and Nebaioth, bring their flocks to the LORD’s altar (Isaiah 60:7).

wordNotes.term: פֶּרֶא אָדָם (pereʾ ʾadam) — a wild man
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “a wild ass of a man.” Pereʾ is the onager, the wild donkey of the arid steppe, celebrated for its freedom and speed. Hosea compares Ephraim to “a wild ass alone by himself,” and Jeremiah uses the animal for Israel’s untamed pursuit of idols. Applied to Ishmael, the figure promises a free, roving, self-reliant life outside settled society.

Literally “upon the face of.” The phrase can denote location (“before,” “east of”) or opposition (“in defiance of, over against”). The law about a firstborn son uses it of preferring one son over another, and Genesis 25:18 repeats it of Ishmael’s descendants. Here the sense of living in tension with his kin best suits the preceding lines.

verses.bibleText: And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me: for she said, Have I also here looked after him that seeth me?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Hagar’s response is not to the promise of a son but to the One who gave it. “She called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me.” The narrator states plainly that it was “the LORD” who spoke to her, confirming that the Angel was the LORD present in revelation. And Hagar does something no other person in Scripture does: she gives God a name. Others call upon his name or name places after him, but this Egyptian slave woman, newly met by grace, coins a title for him out of her own experience: El Roʾi, “a God of seeing.”

The name holds two ideas together. He is the God who sees her, who noticed her affliction when no one in Abram’s household did. He is also, in her astonished experience, a God who allows himself to be seen. Her explanation, “Have I also here looked after him that seeth me?”, is notoriously difficult in Hebrew. It may mean “Have I really seen, here, the One who sees me?” or, taking “after” in the sense of “the back of,” “Have I here seen the back of him who sees me?” That second reading would link her experience with Moses, who was permitted to see God’s back but not his face (Exodus 33:20–23). Either way, Hagar marvels that she has encountered God and lived. Fallen human beings cannot behold the full glory of God (Exodus 33:20; John 1:18), yet God condescends to make himself known in a form his creatures can bear. That is precisely the ministry the Angel of the LORD foreshadows and that is fulfilled when the Word becomes flesh and dwells among us (John 1:14).

The change in Hagar is striking. At the beginning of the chapter she looked at her mistress with contempt because she had conceived. Now her attention has moved from her pregnancy to her God. She no longer measures herself by what she can produce but by the fact that she has been seen and addressed by the LORD.

The name “Thou God seest me” is both comfort and searching. To the afflicted it means that no tear goes unnoticed (Psalm 56:8). To the proud it means that nothing is hidden (Hebrews 4:13). Hagar knew both: she had despised her mistress and been afflicted by her, and the God who saw everything sent her back with mercy.

wordNotes.term: אֵל רֳאִי (El Roʾi) — Thou God seest me
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “God of seeing” or “God of my seeing.” The Hebrew can be understood as “the God who sees me” or “the God whom I have seen,” and the context lets both resonate. The Septuagint renders it “the God who looked upon me,” emphasizing God’s regard for Hagar. Elsewhere Scripture celebrates the LORD whose eyes run to and fro throughout the earth and who looks on the lowly.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi; behold, it is between Kadesh and Bered.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The encounter is fixed in geography. “Wherefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi,” that is, “the well of the Living One who sees me.” Hagar’s experience becomes a landmark, and those who later drew water there would be reminded that the living God had met a fugitive at that spot. Notably, the name commemorates God’s seeing rather than Hagar’s: the emphasis falls on his gracious initiative toward her, not on any distinction she had gained.

The location is given as “between Kadesh and Bered.” Kadesh, usually identified with Kadesh-barnea, lay in the northern Sinai on the southern edge of Canaan. Bered appears nowhere else, and the well cannot be identified with confidence today. The place reappears in the story, however, as a home of Isaac (24:62; 25:11). The child of promise later lived beside the well where God revealed himself to the mother of Ishmael, a quiet sign that the God of the one line had not forgotten the other.

wordNotes.term: בְּאֵר לַחַי רֹאִי (Beʾer Laḥai Roʾi) — Beer-lahai-roi
wordNotes.explanation: “Well of the Living One who sees me.” Beʾer denotes a well or cistern, perhaps dug near the spring (ʿayin) of verse 7. Ḥai, “living,” is used of God as the living God, distinct from lifeless idols. The name joins God’s life with his watchful care.

verses.bibleText: And Hagar bare Abram a son: and Abram called his son's name, which Hagar bare, Ishmael.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Hagar obeyed. She returned, and the narrative resumes in Abram’s household: “Hagar bare Abram a son.” The sentence answers verse 1 directly. Sarai “bare him no children”; Hagar “bare Abram a son.” The frame closes, but not as Sarai intended. Sarai’s name is entirely absent from these last two verses. She hoped to be built up through the child, yet the text records that the son was borne to Abram, and it is Abram who names him.

“Abram called his son’s name, which Hagar bare, Ishmael.” Abram gives the name God had chosen, which implies that Hagar told him of her encounter at the well and that he accepted it as a word from the LORD. By naming the boy, Abram formally acknowledges him as his own son. For thirteen years Abram seems to have regarded Ishmael as the promised heir; his plea in 17:18, “O that Ishmael might live before thee!”, shows how much he loved the boy.

Paul reads this birth as a figure in Galatians 4. The son of the bondwoman was born “after the flesh,” through human arrangement; the son of the freewoman was born “by promise” (Galatians 4:22–23). Paul is not denying Ishmael’s worth as a person or God’s care for him. He uses the two births to illustrate two ways of relating to God: seeking the inheritance by human effort or receiving it as a gift of grace. Every attempt to secure God’s promises by our own works produces an Ishmael, real and loved yet not the heir of promise. The true heir comes only by the power of God.

wordNotes.explanation: From qaraʾ, “to call, name.” In Genesis the right to name expresses recognition and authority. The Angel told Hagar that she would call him Ishmael, and Abram here performs the act, publicly owning the child as his son while honouring the name God gave. The same verb records Abraham naming Isaac.

verses.bibleText: And Abram was fourscore and six years old, when Hagar bare Ishmael to Abram.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abram was fourscore and six years old, when Hagar bare Ishmael to Abram.” The chronological note anchors the story in Abram’s life. He was seventy-five on entering Canaan (12:4) and is now eighty-six. The next time God speaks to him, he will be ninety-nine (17:1), a silence of thirteen years. Genesis records no revelation in that interval.

The silence may itself be instructive. Abram had tried to hasten the promise, and God now lets him wait longer still, until every natural hope is gone and Isaac’s birth will be unmistakably a work of God (Romans 4:19–21; Hebrews 11:11–12). The waiting was not abandonment. The God who had seen Hagar at the well was still watching over Abram’s tent, and his promise stood unchanged.

wordNotes.term: בֶּן־שְׁמֹנִים שָׁנָה וְשֵׁשׁ שָׁנִים (ben-shemonim shanah weshesh shanim) — fourscore and six years old
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “a son of eighty years and six years,” the ordinary Hebrew idiom for age. Genesis marks Abram’s years at key turning points, letting the reader measure the long delay between promise and fulfilment.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: When God’s promise seems slow, what shortcuts look reasonable to us, and what do they cost?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Human schemes to hurry God’s promise produce strife and suffering, yet the LORD who sees and hears seeks out the wounded and remains faithful to his word.
discussionQuestions: Why did Sarai’s proposal seem sensible in her culture, and why was it still a failure of faith?
How do the words “hearkened to the voice” and “took … and gave” recall Genesis 3?
What does the Angel’s question “whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go?” ask of Hagar, and of us?
How can God command Hagar to return and submit while also declaring that he has heard her affliction?
What does Hagar learn about God at the well, and why does she name the place for his seeing rather than her own?
commonMisunderstandings: The chapter does not approve of the surrogate arrangement simply because it was customary; the narrative traces its bitter results.
God’s instruction to return does not excuse Sarai’s harshness or make mistreatment acceptable.
The description of Ishmael in verse 12 is not a license to stereotype any modern people.
Ishmael is not rejected from God’s care; he receives real blessing even though the covenant line runs through Isaac.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold together the honesty of the narrative about Abram and Sarai’s failure and the tenderness of the LORD toward the slave woman whom everyone else used and none addressed by name.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Wait for the LORD rather than forcing his promises, and when you are the one who has fled, listen for the voice that calls you by name and sends you back with hope.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God fulfills his promises by grace and in his own time, and the same God seeks, sees, and hears the lost and afflicted.
flow: Abram and Sarai tried to obtain the promised heir by their own arrangement, and the result was strife.
Paul treats this birth “after the flesh” as a picture of every attempt to gain God’s blessing by human effort.
In contrast, the LORD himself goes looking for the runaway slave and calls her by name.
He hears affliction, gives promises, and reveals himself as the God who sees.
Christ is still the Seeker who finds the lost and calls them home to rest in his promise.
simpleIllustrations: A child who cannot wait for a gift and takes a substitute from the shelf often finds the substitute brings trouble, while the gift still comes on the appointed day.
A traveler alone on a desert road who hears her own name spoken by a stranger knows she has not been forgotten.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you stop trying to secure God’s blessing by your own plans and trust the God who sees you and has promised to provide?
cautions: Do not caricature Hagar, Sarai, or Abram; each is drawn with both fault and pathos.
Do not use verse 12 to disparage Arab or Muslim neighbours; the oracle concerns Ishmael and his line in the biblical setting.
Do not imply that God’s command to return endorses abuse; the LORD who sent Hagar back also heard her affliction and protected her future.

reflectionQuestions: Where am I tempted to help God keep a promise by a plan he has not given me?
When my choices bring conflict, do I own my part or, like Sarai and Abram, shift the blame?
How have I treated people who have less power than I do in my home, church, or work?
If the LORD asked me today, “whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go?”, how would I answer?
What difference does it make to me that God sees me even when I feel unseen by everyone else?
